result: The authors validated their pipette cleaning protocol by comparing cellular and synaptic properties of neurons recorded before and after cleaning in both rat and human tissue. They found no systematic changes in properties like resting membrane potential, input resistance, spontaneous EPSP frequency/amplitude, and action potential kinetics after up to two cleaning cycles, with mean relative differences between 0-10% and p>0.05 for all comparisons.
evaluation: Reviewers raised a major concern (Essential revision #1) that the authors 'omitted' the aCSF rinsing step from the original Forest protocol and provided 'little or no data' to support this practice. They specifically requested data on 'how the membrane potential, input resistance, synaptic events, and action potential parameters change over time after patching and repatching.' While the authors provided extensive validation data in rat tissue (C36-C38, C167) and some human tissue comparisons (C168-C174), the reviewers' concern about the omitted rinsing step and request for temporal dynamics suggests the validation was incomplete or not fully convincing in the initial submission.

result: The authors developed multipatch setups with 6, 8, and 10 manipulators, achieving success rates of 88±12%, 85±13%, and 79±11% respectively, with corresponding average tested connections of 23±7, 41±13, and 56±17. They implemented semi-automated pipette positioning and prefilling approaches to reduce experimental time, though success rates decreased and experimental time increased (from 36.6±2.3 to 46.1±4.6 min) as the number of pipettes increased.
evaluation: The reviewers acknowledged the methodology was 'well laid out, with appropriate drawings, photos, parts lists, and videos' and should be 'an accessible method.' The acceptance summary explicitly states the authors 'show their robotic system can obtain high numbers of successful paired recordings.' No specific concerns were raised about the performance metrics or setup configurations, indicating reviewer acceptance of these technical achievements.

result: The clean-to-complete strategy increased average cluster size on 8- and 10-pipette setups to 7.8±0.4 (97±5% success rate) and 9.2±0.6 (92±6% success rate) respectively. Pipettes from failed recording attempts could be immediately cleaned and reused, even simultaneously with ongoing patch attempts, greatly increasing the success rate and yield of experiments.
evaluation: The acceptance summary explicitly states the system 'can obtain high numbers of successful paired recordings in part due to a system that allows for cleaning and reusing patch electrodes for multiple serial recordings.' The reviewers acknowledged this as a key innovation and did not raise concerns about the clean-to-complete performance metrics, indicating acceptance of these results.

result: Using both cleaning strategies (clean-to-complete and clean-to-extend), the authors increased tested connections from 140±24 to 244±52 per animal in rodent experiments. In human tissue, they recorded up to 17 neighboring neurons in one slice and up to 99 neurons probing 300-700 connections from individual patients within 24 hours. The distance distribution remained similar across sequential recording rounds, and the approach could unveil complex connectivity patterns beyond simple pairwise statistics.
evaluation: The acceptance summary states the approach 'yields hundreds of potential neural pairs per patient sample, which will undoubtedly yield novel insights.' Reviewers requested clarification on experimental details (Essential revision #3) including 'the time that is taken to probe connectivity and an analysis of the distance distribution,' which the authors appear to have addressed (C94). The overall throughput achievements were accepted as demonstrated.

result: The method enabled probing of 150 synaptic connections between 17 neurons in one human slice and screening of over 600 connections from single patients. Excitatory connectivity between pyramidal cells in human layer 2/3 ranged from 12.9-17.7%, similar to previous reports, with inter-individual differences not statistically different from each other. Sample sizes from single patients were comparable to datasets generated by pooling multiple subjects, representing a substantial increase in performance.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the high throughput, they raised concerns about connectivity analysis. Essential revision #2 states 'The article overemphasizes connectivity analysis and ignores its limitations, e.g., false negatives' and suggests emphasizing that multipatch is 'currently the only technique available to assay the strength and short-term plasticity of monosynaptic connectivity.' Essential revision #5 questions whether the data will be 'sufficient yet to probe the difference between individuals' and suggests the authors 'tone down this claim.' This indicates reviewer uncertainty about the connectivity findings and their interpretation.

result: The authors developed an automated pressure system that can be built within a week with basic equipment, using specific pressure settings (20 mbar LOW, 70 mbar HIGH) for different experimental phases. The system is applicable to any patch-clamp setup and can reduce experimental errors, increase speed, and help experimenters concentrate on essential tasks.
evaluation: The acceptance summary explicitly mentions 'automated pressure control' as one of the 'recent innovations' the authors 'adopted and optimized.' The reviewers stated the methodology was 'well laid out' and should be accessible, with no specific concerns raised about the pressure system design or implementation.

result: The semi-automated approach achieved higher success rates (88%/85%/79%) compared to fully automated systems (43-51%) and was faster for pipette positioning (53/55 s vs 103 s per pipette), though slightly slower for approaching cells and establishing whole-cell configuration (126/154 s vs 120 s). The authors concluded that fully automated multipatch would require disproportionate effort and that slice exchange and cell selection would still require human presence.
evaluation: The acceptance summary describes the method as 'semi-automated' and reviewers acknowledged the 'benefits of the semi-automated approach' (Essential revision #4). The comparison with fully automated systems and the rationale for the semi-automated design were not challenged, indicating reviewer acceptance of this approach and its performance advantages.

result: Automated data analysis is an essential step to leverage the increased experimental throughput. A previous study demonstrated an automatic synapse detection algorithm using a support vector machine classifier that achieved 95% accuracy.
evaluation: Essential revision #4 states that authors 'do not identify other aspects of multipatch experiments that could benefit from automation – for example, data acquisition and online QC, and real-time connection detection.' The reviewers also noted that 'With the potential for so much data gathering, data format (e.g. Neurodata without borders), data sharing, automation of connection detection and analysis, should be addressed.' This indicates the reviewers felt these aspects were insufficiently addressed in the original submission.

result: The authors discussed limitations of slice experiments including underestimation of synaptic connectivity due to axon cutting, with correction factors ranging from 1.1-1.7 reported in different studies. They noted that in vivo recordings found 6.7% connection probability compared to 9.3% in slices, and emphasized the importance of avoiding superficial cells, controlling for intersomatic distances, and ensuring good recording quality.
evaluation: Essential revision #2 explicitly requested that authors address connectivity analysis limitations, stating 'The article overemphasizes connectivity analysis and ignores its limitations, e.g., false negatives.' The inclusion of this extensive discussion of limitations and methodological considerations (C113-C119) appears to address this concern, and the acceptance summary indicates the overall approach was validated, suggesting these limitations were adequately discussed in revision.
